question: Your application receives each of these stop_reason values from the Messages API. Choose the correct handling for each.
choices: Run the tools and send tool_result blocks
Send the assistant content back to continue
Check stop_details; retry on a fallback model

rows.note: Claude finished naturally.

rows.answer: Run the tools and send tool_result blocks
rows.note: Your code executes client tools and returns the results.

rows.answer: Send the assistant content back to continue
rows.note: A server-tool loop hit its iteration limit; resend the assistant content as-is.
Raise max_tokens or continue the response.
The response filled the context window; the content is valid but cut off.

rows.answer: Check stop_details; retry on a fallback model
rows.note: Returned as HTTP 200; stop_details names the policy category.

explanation: stop_reason drives the loop; only tool_use needs your tool results, and pause_turn comes from server tools.

question: Choose the API for each workload.

rows.text: Summarise 10,000 documents overnight for a report read the next morning.
rows.note: Latency-tolerant volume at 50% of the cost, within 24 hours.

rows.text: A chat assistant inside the product that users wait on.
rows.note: Someone is waiting for each answer.

rows.text: Run a 5,000-prompt regression eval after each prompt change.
rows.note: Evals are a standard batch workload.

rows.text: An agent that calls your client-side tools and needs each result before its next step.
rows.note: Batch requests run independently, so your tool loop cannot run inside one.

rows.text: A healthcare customer under zero data retention needs cheaper nightly summaries.
rows.note: The Batch API is not ZDR-eligible; use the Messages API with prompt caching.

explanation: Ask first whether anyone is waiting and whether the work needs a live tool loop; then check data-retention constraints.

question: Choose the best way to give Claude each capability.

rows.text: Several Claude applications need the same internal inventory service, maintained by one team.
rows.note: One reusable server, many clients.

rows.text: A single app needs Claude to call one internal pricing function in its own codebase.
rows.note: A tool definition with a clear schema, executed by your app.

rows.text: A documented, multi-step procedure for preparing a release, with templates.
rows.note: Instructions and resources that load only when needed.

rows.text: Searching the public web for current information.
rows.note: Web search is an Anthropic-provided server tool.

rows.text: Editing files and running shell commands in a coding agent.
rows.note: Bash and text-editor tools are Anthropic-defined.

explanation: Built-ins for standard capabilities, custom tools for one app's functions, MCP for reuse across apps, Skills for instructions.

question: Mark each statement about prompt caching true or false.

rows.text: The cache prefix is built in the order tools, then system, then messages.
rows.note: Each level builds on the previous ones.

rows.text: Changing a tool definition invalidates the cached system prompt and messages too.
rows.note: Tool changes invalidate every level after them.

rows.text: Putting the current timestamp at the start of the system prompt does not affect cache hits.
rows.note: Any change before the breakpoint breaks the exact-prefix match.

rows.text: The default cache lifetime is 5 minutes and is refreshed each time the cache is read.
rows.note: A 1-hour TTL is available at a higher write price.

rows.text: A request can have at most 4 explicit cache breakpoints.
rows.note: Automatic caching uses one of the four slots.

rows.text: Cache reads cost more than base input tokens because the cache must be looked up.
rows.note: Reads cost a fraction of base input (0.1× on most models, less on some newer ones); writes cost more.

explanation: Static content first, volatile content after the breakpoint, and keep tool definitions stable.

question: In Claude Code, can a hook on each of these events prevent or block the action?

rows.note: Exit code 2 or permissionDecision deny blocks the tool call.
The tool has already run; feedback only.
The prompt never reaches Claude.
It can keep Claude working instead of stopping.
It can only add context.
Used for side effects; exit codes are ignored.

explanation: To stop a dangerous action, hook it before it happens with PreToolUse; PostToolUse is for reacting afterwards.

question: Is each Claude Code file shared with the team through the repository, or personal to one developer?

rows.note: Shared project settings, committed to git.
Project-local settings, added to git excludes automatically.
User settings for every project on that machine.
Project memory committed with the code.
Project-scoped MCP servers shared through version control.

explanation: Team standards live in committed files; personal overrides live in local or user files, which sit at different precedence levels.
